content: Convergence insufficiency is a binocular vision disorder characterized by a tendency for the eyes to drift outward (exophoria) and difficulty in turning the eyes inward during activities such as reading or performing close-up tasks. This condition can cause significant visual discomfort and symptoms such as eye strain, headaches, and difficulty concentrating. A systematic review and network meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of various non-surgical treatments for convergence insufficiency. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving both children and adults with symptomatic convergence insufficiency. The interventions assessed included: 1. Office-based vergence/accommodative therapy with home reinforcement. 2. Home-based pencil/target push-ups. 3. Home-based computer vergence/accommodative therapy. 4. Office-based vergence/accommodative therapy alone. 5. Placebo vergence/accommodative therapy or other placebo interventions. 6. Prism reading glasses. 7. Placebo reading glasses. Findings in Children: A total of six RCTs involving 968 children were included, with four trials conducted by the Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial (CITT) Investigator Group. These trials were rated as having a low risk of bias and used consistent diagnostic criteria and outcome measures. When treatment success was defined as achieving normal clinical measures of convergence and a pre-specified magnitude of improvement, office-based vergence/accommodative therapy with home reinforcement was found to be significantly more effective than: Home-based computer vergence/accommodative therapy (Risk Ratio [RR] 1.96, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.32 to 2.94). Home-based pencil/target push-ups (RR 2.86, 95% CI 1.82 to 4.35). Placebo therapy (RR 3.04, 95% CI 2.32 to 3.98). There was no significant difference in treatment success between home-based computer therapy and home-based pencil push-ups (RR 1.44, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.24), or between either of these home-based therapies and placebo therapy. When treatment success was defined as a composite outcome of convergence improvement and symptom resolution, moderate-certainty evidence showed that office-based vergence/accommodative therapy with home reinforcement was 5.12 times more likely to result in success compared to placebo therapy (95% CI 2.01 to 13.07). Low-certainty evidence suggested that office-based therapy with home reinforcement might be: 4.41 times more effective than home-based pencil push-ups (95% CI 1.26 to 15.38). 4.65 times more effective than home-based computer therapy (95% CI 1.23 to 17.54). No significant differences were found between home-based pencil push-ups, home-based computer therapy, or placebo therapy. One trial evaluated the use of base-in prism reading glasses in children and found no significant differences in near point convergence (NPC), positive fusional vergence (PFV), or symptom scores (measured by the Convergence Insufficiency Symptom Survey [CISS]) when compared to placebo reading glasses. Findings in Adults: Six RCTs involving 321 adults were included, but only one trial was rated as having a low risk of bias. Due to the lack of composite success data in adult studies, network meta-analyses could not be performed for treatment success. Instead, individual outcomes such as NPC, PFV, and CISS scores were analyzed. Office-based vergence/accommodative therapy was found to be more effective than placebo therapy in improving PFV (Mean Difference [MD] 16.73, 95% CI 6.96 to 26.60). However, no significant differences were observed for NPC or CISS scores. No significant differences were found between other interventions for any of the outcomes. One trial evaluated base-in prism glasses for near-work activities and found that participants using prism glasses reported fewer symptoms at three months compared to those using placebo glasses (MD -8.9, 95% CI -11.6 to -6.3). However, no significant differences were observed in NPC or PFV with this intervention. Adherence and Safety: Excellent adherence rates (96.6% or higher) were reported for office-based vergence/accommodative therapy in two trials. In contrast, adherence to home-based therapies was less consistent, with one study reporting a decline in adherence over time (weeks 7 to 12) and lower completion rates for home-based pencil/target push-ups. No adverse effects related to any of the study treatments were reported. Conclusions: In children, office-based vergence/accommodative therapy with home reinforcement is more effective than home-based pencil/target push-ups or home-based computer vergence/accommodative therapy for improving convergence insufficiency. In adults, the evidence regarding the effectiveness of non-surgical interventions is less clear, with limited data supporting the superiority of any specific treatment.
